subject: Clarify tenant-scoped disposition bounds & forensic snapshot proof
messages:
From: Marta Ruiz <marta.ruiz@orchard-health.com>

Cc: security@orchard-health.com, legal@orchard-health.com
Date: Fri, 7 Aug 2026 09:15:00 -0700
Subject: Tenant-scoped disposition bounds and forensics ask

Hi Ben,

We are working through our procurement Security Questionnaire and have a couple of items that need clarification around how Redwood handles customer-specific log retention and forensic snapshots. Two asks: 

1) For tenant-scoped debug/session logs (these are ephemeral by default in our current config), can Orchard request a temporary retention extension for a specific tenant (i.e., 60–90 days) while we complete a regulatory review? If yes, what is the process and who signs off internally?

2) For forensics requests, we need an auditable "proof of delete" workflow and a description of how you produce a locked forensic snapshot (if requested) and then subsequently attest to deletion. Can you provide a short description or example artifacts you would give to a customer?

We prefer short, concrete answers and any evidence (templates, example attestations, sample export filenames) we can attach to our SIG/CAIQ submission.

Thanks — please loop in whoever owns retention policy or forensics on your side.

—Marta
Marta Ruiz
Head of Security Operations
Orchard Health
From: ben_carter@redwood.com
To: Marta Ruiz <marta.ruiz@orchard-health.com>
Cc: karthik_iyer@redwood.com, priya_natarajan@redwood.com
Date: Fri, 7 Aug 2026 10:02:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Tenant-scoped disposition bounds and forensics ask

Marta — thanks for the clear questions. Looping in Karthik (engineering/runtime) and Priya (security/compliance) to provide the specifics. High-level answers below and we can follow up with artifacts. I've attached a retention_matrix.xlsx that we use to map log classes to retention windows; fill in tenant details and we can propose an approval path.

Short answers (TL;DR):
- Temporary tenant retention extensions: Supported. Self-serve for short durations via a support ticket for Hosted customers; for Dedicated/Private we require a signed MA and an internal change request (approval from Product + Security). Max practical short-term window we typically approve is 90 days for ephemeral debug logs; audit logs are handled differently and often retained longer if requested.
- Forensic snapshot & proof-of-delete: We can produce a timeboxed, access-controlled snapshot export (SHA256 checksums for files) and a deletion attestation once the snapshot is removed. The sequence we follow: request acceptance -> create export -> publish hashed manifest -> provide secure download to customer/legal -> delete snapshot from internal storage -> produce signed deletion attestation (PDF) and retention log.

Attachments included: retention_matrix.xlsx (template). Karthik / Priya — can you add tech/process details and an example attestation we can share with Marta?

Thanks,
Ben Carter
Senior Account Executive — Strategic Accounts
Redwood Inference

Hey all — adding the technical detail below. Quoting Ben's summary for context.

On Fri, Aug 7, 2026 at 10:02 AM ben_carter@redwood.com wrote:
> Short answers (TL;DR):
> - Temporary tenant retention extensions: Supported... (see Ben's note)
> - Forensic snapshot & proof-of-delete: We can produce a timeboxed...

Technical/process details (forline):
- Log classes: we separate logs into (1) ephemeral session/tracing (high-volume, per-tenant, default TTL 7–30d), (2) audit/authoritative trails (security events, admin changes; default TTL 365d+), and (3) operational diagnostics (rotated to cold storage).
- Tenant extension mechanics: For Hosted customers, our ops team creates a tenant-scoped retention override flag tied to the tenant id. That flag adjusts the lifecycle policy in the object store for only the tenant's debug bucket prefix. The operation is tracked in our change management system (JIRA: SUP-XXXX). All changes include an expiry timestamp and automatic reversion. For Dedicated/Private, the same flag is applied via config change but requires an internal signoff: Product + Security + Customer Success.
- Forensic snapshot workflow: 1) Create export job that snapshots the tenant prefix to an encrypted export bucket with immutable object lock enabled; 2) Generate manifests (file list + per-file SHA256) and sign with our service key; 3) Provide secure download link or SFTP transfer to the customer/legal team; 4) After transfer, run deletion job that removes snapshot objects and records the deletion event in our retention audit log; 5) Produce signed deletion attestation PDF with the manifest reference, deletion timestamp, operator id, and audit-trace GUID.
- Proof characteristics: manifests are cryptographic hashes plus timestamps; deletion attestation includes internal audit log entries and the signed operator action. We can also provide low-level storage object IDs if needed for customer verification.
- Evidence we can share immediately: sample attestation PDF (redact PII), sample manifest, and a short playbook PDF that documents the flow. See internal playbook: https://docs.redwood.com/internal/retention-playbook#tenant-scope (internal link).

Limitations & controls:
- We do not change retention for other tenants as part of any single request; operations are tenant-scoped.
- For legal holds invoked by a court order, the ops + legal route is used (separate SLA).

I'll attach a short draft forensic_snapshot_proposal.pdf and the retention_matrix.xlsx that Ben added. Priya — please confirm signoff matrix (who signs the attestation and the internal approvers).

—Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Principal Engineer, Serving Runtime
Redwood Inference
